short: Not one wall but eighteen centuries of them, rebuilt by dynasty after dynasty.
full:
Rival states were already building long defensive walls in the Warring States period. After unification the First Emperor sent General Meng Tian north with a reported three hundred thousand men to join the northern sections into a continuous barrier against the Xiongnu — rammed earth, not stone, and almost none of it survives. The Han pushed a line of walls and beacon towers west along the Gansu corridor to guard the Silk Road; later dynasties extended, abandoned or ignored the system according to whether they could buy the steppe off instead.

The wall visible today is overwhelmingly Ming work. After a Mongol force captured a Ming emperor in 1449, the court committed to fortification over campaigning, and from the 1470s built some 8,800 kilometres of brick and stone curtain, garrisoned towers and passes. It never quite did what was asked of it. In 1644 the general commanding Shanhai Pass, facing a rebel army that had already taken Beijing, opened the gate and let the Manchus through.
